item.title: Renegotiating Agreements in Non-Monogamy
item.description:
Relationships

Renegotiating Agreements in Non-Monogamy

Embracing change is an essential skill for non-monogamous partners.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Renegotiating agreements is essential, not a sign of failure, in non-monogamous relationships.
  • Regular check-ins to review agreements foster trust, safety, and ongoing connection.
  • Warmth and curiosity during tough talks help create durable, adaptive relationship agreements.
Source: Evanto / LightFieldStudios

People in new non-monogamous relationships often put a lot of effort into crafting airtight relationship agreements. That might look like, for instance, having conversations about how you’ll prioritize between partners when there are competing demands on your time; how you’ll deal with communication so you’ll be able to stay in touch without being glued to your phone; how you’ll manage disclosure and privacy with multiple partners, and so on.

I’m all for having detailed and thoughtful conversations with your partner(s), but there’s one piece that often gets left out of this conversation: renegotiating agreements. I think people sometimes assume that renegotiating agreements is a sign of failure. But from my perspective, it’s an integral part of the process of making and keeping agreements.

That’s why I encourage my clients to think of the first set of agreements as an experiment; you’re going to try something out, gather information, assess, and develop a new plan that’s informed by what you learned. In fact, I recommend that you put time on the calendar to review the experiment and discuss how it went for all concerned—

The Importance of Incremental Experimentation

In my experience, a process of incremental experimentation is one of the secrets to a well-functioning relationship. Responding to one another as you explore new territory creates safety and trust, which allows for more exploration. That’s a much better strategy than deciding how it has to be and then trying to fit yourself and others into a hypothetical structure.

You can’t anticipate everything from the start, and you don’t need to. You are unique humans with unique emotions, preferences, and desires. You can't know how you will respond to something you haven't tried yet, so try something small, and learn from the experiment. Let success and challenge help you shape the next experiment.

What matters much more than the specific agreements you come to is the process by which you come to them:

  • Can you stay tuned in to what’s true for you, even if your conversation partner feels very differently?
  • Can you stay warm and open to your partner, even if what they have to say is hard for you?
  • Can you get curious about what your partner thinks, even if you’re a little scared of what they might say?

These are high-level challenging relationship skills, and pretty much everyone struggles with them. But the more you can practice staying warm and connected during even quite emotionally charged discussions, the more you’ll invite your partner(s) to bring their best selves to the table. Over time, by responding to each other with warmth and attunement, you’ll develop relationship agreements that are truly durable.

item.title: The Loneliness Epidemic at Work
item.description:
Career

The Loneliness Epidemic at Work

Why are we so lonely at work?

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Loneliness at work is epidemic.
  • Yet it doesn't have to be.
  • Three simple, creative steps can help banish loneliness once and for all.

Everyday folks walk into an office full of people doing all kinds of activities. Some may log into a Zoom or Teams or Slack to connect to their follow co-workers, clients, vendors, and suppliers. Others may be in tons of meetings, texts, conversations, calls, and more. The never-ending connectivity must mean that we are super connected to each other, right? It sure seems that way.

Yet millions of people report feeling more isolated than ever[1].

The surprising truth is that workplace loneliness has very little to do with how many people you're around. Or how many meetings you attend. Or what projects you work on every day.

It has everything to do with whether you feel like you matter.

And that feeling has consequences far beyond morale. Lonely employees are less engaged[2], less creative, less willing to collaborate, and far more likely to quit. So what can we do to counter that loneliness epidemic? It turns out that we can get creative. Here are three creativity investments that can make you less lonely at work and build meaning no matter what you do.

1. Invest in relationships

Now, I know I famously recommend that you do not make friends at work. Millions of downloads and translations into several languages has not been without controversy[3]. Yet friends are far more powerful when you do not have some sort of monetary gain between you, competition for promotion, looking for a competitive edge, and so on at work. Friends instead should be made outside of work at all costs.

But relationships with co-workers? That’s gold.

Relationships at work with people who are long term co-workers and collaborators is an investment worth making and taking seriously. It’s not a friendship per se; it's more of your network.

These relationships are people that you can bond with over a win at work, or a loss, or a crazy client request or a supplier misstep. The connection you make when you build professional relationships can give you more meaning at work no matter what you do, and help you be seen, appreciated, and valued as a member of a team trying to accomplish a shared goal together.

Invest in relationships at work to give your time there more meaning.

2. Invest outside of Work

Most people think that unless they squeeze out every single drop of meaning at work from every single project, client, vendor, conference, work event, or supplier, then they are unfulfilled.

But when we look at this creatively, we flip the paradigm.

Instead of looking to work to give us all this meaning, look outside of work instead. There are several amazing opportunities outside of work to conquer loneliness and make lifelong connections. And a bonus is the ability to make true and genuine friends unlike what you would ever be able to make at work[4].

The secret is volunteer work. Literally anywhere. Your church needs help with ushers and greeters. You Synagogue needs help with the sisterhood brunch on Tuesday. Literally just about every volunteer-based group out there needs some help in some capacity. Yet seldom do folks reach out and volunteer their time[5]. Yet here is where real meaning is often built, and a sense of your role in society at large and among a community of like-minded folks. So take that leap into volunteer work and you may find amazing creative and life-changing benefit.

3. Invest in someone else

Choose one person every day to help make them feel seen at work. It can be anybody. Your boss, your co-worker, a vendor, or even someone on your way to work or the person who you drop off your kids with at the day care.

Get creative with it and make it a system you practice every day[6]. Some ideas may include things like one sincere thank you to someone. A real, heartfelt thank you. One direct and meaningful moment of recognition. One request for someone’s opinion or a moment to ask someone for genuine advice.

Feeling noticed is one of the simplest antidotes to workplace loneliness, and it has the amazing side benefit of being good for you, too. People become happier thought kindness[7]. And the more creative you get with it, the more contagious the energy becomes.

So while we often feel so lonely, especially with technology that promises redemption yet digs us further into loneliness[8], there are things we can do to change the conversation around loneliness and become more meaningfully connected. Volunteer work, investing in making someone else seen, and investing in meaningful real co-worker relationships are only three creative ideas of many on how to counteract the effects of loneliness and give us a sense that we indeed truly matter.

item.title: Does Ozempic Blunt Our Hunger for Love?
item.description:
Mating

Does Ozempic Blunt Our Hunger for Love?

GLP-1 drugs affect more desires than just appetite for food.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • GLP-1 drugs suppress appetite by acting on receptors in the reward and motivation systems in the brain.
  • Evidence is growing that GLP-1 drugs can reduce cravings for addictive substances and behaviours.
  • Reward-seeking behaviour linked to intense infatuation may be affected by GLP-1s, but love is more complex.

Ozempic has stood at the forefront of a group of drugs known as GLP-1 receptor agonists that have since become a global phenomenon.

Originally developed for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, GLP-1s expanded to the management of obesity, before breaking through clinical boundaries and being adopted as lifestyle drugs that otherwise healthy individuals use for weight loss.

Uptake became so enthusiastic that stock shortages of the major brands (Ozempic, Mounjaro, Wegovy) hit in 2022, when supply couldn’t keep up with social-media-fueled demand. Demand was so high that one man and his brother famously built a billion-dollar telehealth company selling independently formulated versions of the drugs.

We now find ourselves in the middle of a giant, ungoverned sociomedical experiment. The widespread use of these drugs means all the risks and unintended side effects of “cosmetic pharmacology” are now being uncovered at scale.

One important discovery is that these drugs control more appetites than just food.

How GLP-1 drugs suppress appetite

GLP-1 drugs work by mimicking a class of natural peptides called incretins that are released from the gut wall to coordinate the body’s response to feeding. Incretins promote insulin release, slow gastric emptying, and suppress appetite. They shift the body into a state optimised for digestion and absorption of nutrients, and reduce the desire to seek more food.

GLP-1 drugs are synthetic forms of this natural biochemical signal, but they last longer in the body, prolonging the feeling of being sated.

The appetite suppression mechanism is not primarily located in the gut, however. Incretin receptors are found throughout the brain's reward and motivation systems.

Importantly, these neural systems don’t just regulate physiological responses to food; they also regulate the hedonic pleasure of foods—determining how palatable they are, and how motivated we are to seek them.

Incretins suppress appetite by inhibiting the dopamine-based “wanting” drive that makes us seek out delicious foods, and decreasing the strength of desire we feel for them.

Of course, these reward and motivation pathways in the brain don’t just control desire for food. They regulate many other hedonic drives—including the compulsive desires seen in drug and alcohol addictions (Kenny, 2011). The potential of incretin receptors to moderate cravings has opened up a whole new avenue for the treatment of substance use disorders with GLP-1 drugs.

Preliminary results are encouraging, suggesting that suppression of motivation and reward seeking can reduce substance use severity in addicts (Dawid et al., 2026).

How many desires are suppressed?

It’s becoming clear that GLP-1 drugs can reduce both appetite for food and dysregulated drives like binge-eating, alcohol or drug misuse. Naturally enough, attention is broadening out to their potential for also managing behavioural addictions linked to gambling, shopping, or sex.

A recent paper (Arillotta et al, 2024) searched the same social media ecosystem that promoted uptake of these drugs in the first place to look for clues—analysing Reddit posts on the behavioural changes reported by people taking GLP-1 drugs. The results suggest a reduction in compulsive use of alcohol, caffeine, nicotine and shopping, but a possible increase in libido.

This last point highlights broader concerns about just how many hedonic drives might be affected. Disquiet is growing about the potential wider impact of these drugs on natural rewards, including romantic love.

This is not a baseless concern. A general suppression of desire, of wanting, should impact wanting another person too, and the insatiable desire, euphoric highs, and intrusive thoughts of early love share a lot of similarities with a behavioural addiction.

But love, as has often been observed, is a many-splendored thing. It is not just about reward seeking.

There are layers of psychological and neurobiological complexity in romantic connection: libido, attraction, attachment, bonding, trust, care, affection. How GLP-1 drugs interact with all these factors is largely unknown, and confounded further by the psychological impact that losing weight has on body image, self-confidence, and general health.

Ultimately, we will only learn how all these influences interact to affect love once the results from the uncontrolled social experiment become clear.

From what we know so far, a cautious prediction might be that GLP-1 drugs would have most impact on the insatiable, euphoric, involuntary forms of love—such as limerence—that are driven by reward-seeking behaviour. Or perhaps these drugs will subtly shift the relative contributions of lust, attraction and attachment that compose the complex feelings of love we have for a romantic partner.

At this stage, it remains to be seen how significant any of these secondary psychological consequences of weight loss are for the wellbeing of both individuals and society.

Time will tell.

item.title: Theory as the Critical Ingredient of Clinical Practice
item.description:
Psychological Evaluation

Theory as the Critical Ingredient of Clinical Practice

Professionals apply theory whereas technicians use only tips and tricks.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Professionals require the application of theory to all cases to meet the needs of all clients.
  • Theory promotes service delivery to diverse clients, whereas tips and tips limit the scope of services.
  • Professionals use theory to organize and evaluate their tips and tricks. Technicians only use tips and tricks.

For nearly every professional continuing education workshop and graduate class in psychology, someone will be overheard evaluating the quality of the educational experience by whether the information contained is practical or theoretical. Practical is good, clear, and useful. Theoretical is esoteric and not useful. This strikes me as exactly the wrong framing. Certainly, there is the Lewin quote that "there is nothing so practical as a good theory." Beyond that, eschewing theory in professional development or even pre-practice professional preparation leads to an approach to clinical practice that is bad for service delivery, bad for clients and patients, and bad for professional credibility. Theory is not something to be suffered through in graduate school. Theory is the critical ingredient in quality clinical practice and requires renewed emphasis at all levels of training.

Why Tips and Tricks Are Not Enough for Quality Clinical Practice

Being a professional psychologist is far more than implementing a collection of tips and tricks. Tips and tricks are those little procedures, processes, or ideas that can be immediately applied to specific settings and specific situations. As we become more experienced, we collect new therapy techniques, new assessment techniques, time savers, and shortcuts like a carpenter who collects a variety of hammers. But sometimes the problem is not a nail.

My first big case working in a hospital was a favor for a friend of one of our surgeons. They needed a good assessment of cognitive functioning to see the best way to teach this child, or if this child could learn at all before the family moved. I was new and did not have a caseload yet. So I scrambled a WISC (i.e., Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children) kit and prepared for a standardized assessment of intelligence. The intake information came to me 30 minutes before the appointment (typically, I receive this information many days in advance). The child was blind, hydrocephalic, non-ambulatory, and nonverbal. All previous attempts by psychologists received a "not testable" conclusion. Knowing the tips and tricks of how to administer, score, and interpret a standardized test of intelligence is often useful, but not in this case. Yet understanding theory allowed me to quickly develop a measure of classical conditioning (pairing a bell and a palm touch), second-order conditioning, operant conditioning, adaptive behavior interviewing of caregivers, and rudimentary Piagetian tasks. This was not a test yielding numbers for a bureaucratic purpose (e.g., eligibility for an educational program) but an assessment that answered the presenting question. Without theory, this child would continue to carry the useless "not testable" designation.

article continues after advertisement

Tips and tricks tend to be a one-size-fits-most approach to clinical work. Often, these are evidence-based approaches such as manualized interventions, novel therapy techniques, or application of new and well-developed tests. Sometimes a continuing education approach to tips and tricks involves someone armed with a great website, charisma, a large speaking fee, snake oil, and non-disclosure agreements for workshop participants. Evidence is non-existent or limited to testimonials (which does not constitute evidence of effectiveness), but the information seems practical, seems to be an answer to a difficult problem, and seems to be "simply common sense." Tips and tricks may be evidence-based, but sometimes not.

How Theory Enhances Professionalism and Individualized Client Care

Quality theory guides hypotheses and predictions, novel approaches to applications, consideration of cultural and contextual variations, and professionalism. Focusing on theory allows for individualized clinical work to best meet the needs of clientele. Client needs are frequently defined by psychologists as what tips and tricks that the psychologist has mastered, not the true needs of the client. For example, after an assessment, the psychologist declared that the client needs exactly the form of cognitive behavioral therapy that the psychologist is an expert in. Knowing if this is the true client need is impossible, but it is often defined as such. Professionals solve complex problems with skills, knowledge, and professional and ethical judgment, and technicians only possess an array of skills that they try to apply to all clients in a Procrustean manner. The focus entirely on tips and tricks defines psychologists engaging in clinical practice as technicians and not professionals.

Relevant research requires the testing and building of theory. Much research is empirical and without a strong theoretical foundation. Clinicians require a coherent approach to compiling research for it to be useful. Research without a theoretical foundation often evaluates tips and tricks. But this is like trying to build a house that is useful and structured, but simply making bricks without architecture, design, or construction skills to erect the house. We often have a pile of well-made bricks with restricted usefulness, and are not much closer to having a useful house.

article continues after advertisement

Credible and professional psychology is responsive to the needs of all patients and clients. Evidence-based practices are necessary, but not sufficient. For example, most published research excludes outliers in their program evaluations. Yet, what researchers call outliers, clinicians call clients. Strong theory provides guidelines for flexible and responsive practices that are required by professional psychologists.

We all need specific skills, tips, and tricks. We cannot function without a large and growing quiver of up-to-date skills. Yet, an emphasis on theory provides an approach to organizing these skills into a coherent and useful body of knowledge. The best introduction to new tips and tricks involves couching these new skills in the context of theory. Then theory provides guidelines for modifying and individualizing evidence-based approaches and techniques to meet the individual needs of diverse clientele and their families in the context of their culture and other aspects of the systems in which they function. The difference between what professionals do that technicians cannot is theory.

item.title: Eating Disorders in Disguise
item.description:
Eating Disorders

Eating Disorders in Disguise

Why eating disorders are so often missed.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Eating disorders don’t have a “look”—they can affect anyone, in any body.
  • Praise for “healthy habits” can mask serious eating disorder behaviors.
  • Physical damage from eating disorders can happen long before visible signs appear.

"You're so disciplined."

"I wish I had your willpower."

"You look amazing. What's your secret?"

These comments are usually intended as compliments. Yet for many people struggling with an eating disorder, they have the potential to reinforce the very behaviors that are causing harm and make it even harder for others to recognize that something is wrong.

As a therapist who specializes in eating disorders and body image concerns, I've had countless clients tell me, "No one knew I was struggling because everyone thought I was doing great." They were praised for losing weight, eating "clean," exercising regularly, or appearing to have incredible self-control. At the same time, they were consumed by thoughts about food and weight, trapped by rigid rules and compulsions. One of the biggest misconceptions about eating disorders is that they are obvious. In reality, they frequently remain hidden behind behaviors that our culture tends to admire.

Why We Miss Them

  • Our culture rewards disordered behaviors. We live in a culture that frequently blurs the line between wellness and disordered eating. Skipping meals can be seen as intermittent fasting, exercising despite pain and exhaustion as a sign of dedication, and carefully tracking every bite of food as evidence of discipline and dedication to health. None of these behaviors is inherently problematic on its own. The issue is that our culture tends to automatically reward weight loss, food restriction, and extreme discipline around eating and exercise, which can make it much harder to recognize when someone is in the depths of any eating disorder. In some cases, the very behaviors that signal an eating disorder are the same ones being celebrated.
  • They don't always fit the stereotype. Many people still imagine someone with an eating disorder as extremely thin, visibly unwell, and refusing to eat. Unfortunately, that stereotype causes many people to go unnoticed and untreated. Eating disorders occur in people of all body sizes, ages, genders, and backgrounds. Someone can be in a larger body, an average-size body, or appear outwardly healthy and still be struggling significantly. In fact, some people receive increasing praise as they become sicker simply because they have lost weight. The emotional distress and medical consequences frequently remain invisible because eating disorders are mental illnesses, not body types.

Shame Keeps People Silent

Source: Taylor Smith / Unsplash

Shame is another reason eating disorders so often go unnoticed. Many people feel embarrassed by their eating behaviors, distressed by changes in their bodies, or ashamed that thoughts about food and weight occupy so much of their mental energy. As a result, they become very skilled at hiding what they are going through. Friends, family members, and even healthcare providers may have no idea that someone is struggling because the person appears successful, high-functioning, and put together on the outside. Sometimes people don't fully recognize the severity of their own symptoms because so many disordered behaviors have become normalized in our culture.

article continues after advertisement

Bias and Misinformation

These misconceptions don't only exist in the general public. They also affect healthcare settings. Eating disorders are frequently overlooked in men, people in midlife and beyond, people in larger bodies, and individuals who are not visibly underweight. Delayed diagnoses are especially common among BIPOC, LGBTQIA+, disabled, and higher-weight individuals, many of whom spend years struggling before receiving appropriate support. When providers rely on stereotypes instead of looking at a person's relationship with food, exercise, and body image, opportunities for early intervention are often missed.

Why This Matters

Eating disorders are serious illnesses that affect both physical and emotional health, and the consequences can be significant even when someone does not appear visibly ill.

Medical complications can include:

  • Low heart rate, low blood pressure, and dangerous electrolyte disturbances
  • Gastrointestinal problems, including bloating, constipation, and slowed digestion
  • Hormonal disruption, fertility issues, and decreased bone density
  • Difficulty concentrating, mood changes, and cognitive impairment
  • Dental and esophageal damage related to purging behaviors

The emotional consequences can be equally serious:

  • Persistent anxiety, depression, or irritability
  • Obsessive thoughts about food, weight, and appearance
  • Social withdrawal and isolation
  • Self-worth that becomes tied to eating habits or body size
  • Rigid thinking that makes asking for help feel impossible

Many people continue to work, care for their families, maintain relationships, and appear to function normally while experiencing severe emotional and physical suffering. Because eating disorders are often hidden behind a veneer of success or discipline, they can go undetected for years.

What This Can Look Like

article continues after advertisement
Source: Jan Sedivy / Unsplash

An eating disorder may look like a teenager who is praised for "eating clean" and rapidly losing weight, a woman in midlife who becomes increasingly anxious about eating anything she considers unhealthy, an athlete who feels unable to rest despite injury and exhaustion, or a man who binge-eats in secret and believes his struggles stem from a lack of willpower. It may also look like someone who appears calm, successful, and completely put together while privately feeling consumed by thoughts about food and their body.

What to Watch for Instead

Rather than asking whether someone looks sick, it is often more helpful to consider how they seem to feel around food and in their body. Some signs that deserve attention include:

  • Rigid food rules or intense anxiety around eating
  • Guilt or shame after meals
  • Avoiding social situations involving food
  • Distress related to body changes or weight
  • A fixation on food, exercise, weight, or appearance
  • Frequent body checking or comparison
  • Cycles of restriction and binge eating
  • Using food or exercise to cope with difficult emotions

Final Thoughts

One of the most challenging aspects of eating disorders is that they often hide behind behaviors that are praised and reinforced by our culture. The person who appears disciplined, healthy, or highly motivated may be struggling profoundly. By moving beyond stereotypes and becoming more curious about people's relationships with food, exercise, and their bodies, we become better equipped to recognize these illnesses earlier and connect people with the support they need.

item.title: How to Stop Saving Your Life for Later
item.description:
Attention

How to Stop Saving Your Life for Later

We've been handed infinite everything; it's making us worse at having any of it.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • More choice doesn't free you; it strands you, less able to pick and less happy with whatever you finally grab.
  • Every time you save something to enjoy later, you feel it less right now.
  • Your brain chases harder than it savors, so you can keep grabbing forever and enjoy almost none of it.

It's Saturday morning, and I'm on the hunt again.

Headphones on, coffee going cold, a few hours deep in the corners of the internet where the music almost nobody has found lives. Right now it's an artist with only 202 monthly listeners, a producer in a tiny bedroom somewhere in Lisbon or Leeds, and it is, I'm certain, one of the most beautiful things I've heard in months. I tap Save. Ah, a vein of gold. The album drops into a library of about 10,000 others, most of which I've played exactly once—or maybe never at all.

I listen to a preposterous amount of music, more than anyone I know, and I can't keep up with my own collecting. The saving of songs has outrun the listening so badly that my own library has become a room full of strangers.

I promise I'm not writing about this because I think my music habit is remotely interesting! I'm mentioning it because it's the most naked version I have of something I'm fairly sure you are doing, too.

We have been handed an all-you-can-eat buffet of everything ever made, and we have learned to stand at it and fill our plates with food we'll never eat, while the meal already in front of us goes cold. That is the bargain almost nobody mentions: Hand a person infinite content, and watch them slowly lose the ability to consume any of it.

The problem with a buffet

There was a famous afternoon in a California grocery store that explains this trap. Researchers set out a tasting table filled with 24 gourmet jams. On other days, at the same table, they put out only six jars. The big display pulled the bigger crowd, the way abundance always does. But the shoppers who encountered six jams were about 10 times more likely to actually buy one—and they walked away happy with the jam they chose. The ones drowning in 24 options mostly tasted, marveled, and left empty-handed.

And that's one issue with a buffet. More options pull us in and then strand us, less able to choose and less satisfied with whatever we finally end up with. Streaming music didn't free me. It handed me 24 million jams and a Save button, and the Save button is now how I cope with overwhelming choice. Every tap is a way of not choosing, of keeping the entire table without committing to a single jar.

Why we can't stop saving

There's a reason the saving itself feels so good, and it has nothing to do with willpower. The brain runs wanting and liking on two different neural systems. Wanting is the chase, the lean-forward, pull-toward something you haven't yet reached. Liking is the slower pleasure of actually having it. The chase is the more powerful system of the two, the one evolved to keep you reaching, and it turns out that the hit of wanting fires whether or not the liking ever arrives. So you can keep grabbing forever and savor nothing.

I have a hunch that my album-saving is never really about only the listening, so much as the reach for something unfamiliar and new. My Saturday hunt is hours of pure, undiluted wanting, running on its own track, often never touching the music I actually play the rest of the week.

The cost of the save

In another study, participants were escorted through an art museum and told to photograph some objects and to simply observe others. The next day, people remembered the photographed objects worse. They remembered fewer of them, in less detail. The act of saving the thing, capturing it to keep, made them experience it less. They had handed the moment to the camera and subconsciously checked out of it.

But there was a twist! When people zoomed in—when they paid close, deliberate attention to just one part of an object before they snapped a photo—the impairment disappeared. Like magic, their memory came back, even for the parts they never framed. Turns out, the real kind of attention undid the damage of thoughtless saving.

So saving is not neutral. Reach for the bookmark or the Save-for-Later button and you don't just push the experience off to a later that rarely comes. You actually thin out the experience you're having right now. It's like every save is a tiny act of leaving the room you're sitting in.

Is it ever about the music?

For years I filed my library under harmless eccentricity, the music obsessive with an insatiable appetite. Then I started seeing the same things everywhere else in my life. The hardcover books I buy that remain unread on the shelf. The people I keep meaning to call, who sit in a mental queue that runs a lot like my Spotify library—full of names I love and rarely reach.

Now stay with the music for a second, because it shows a pattern most clearly. When I open the library, I keep running into the same small, disorienting encounter. There's an album I clearly loved once, saved by a version of me who had a reason, and I can't for the life of me reconstruct the reason. I don't remember the night I found it, what sent me searching, or what it even sounds like. The taste is unmistakably mine, but the memory of ever using it is gone.

That makes a certain kind of sense, given how the saving works. The reach fires, I grab for it, the album drops into the library, and because the wanting never had to become any actual listening, it leaves almost nothing behind in me. A save is the residue of a want that never became a having. No wonder I can't account for it. There was never a moment to remember, only the moment of reaching for it.

Now do that same calculus with the unread books on the shelf or your uncalled friends sitting in the mental queue, and the hobby that got out of hand shows its true shape: a library, and then a life, curated in obsessive detail by someone you can no longer fully account for. You become the collector of a life you aren't quite living, carried from one save to the next by a current you never agreed to.

An album will wait. It sits in the library exactly where I left it, the same song one tap away in a year—or in 10. The people in the mental queue don't wait like that. They get older, they move away, and some of them stop wondering why I never called. The save button taught me that everything can be kept and returned to later, and I never noticed it was lying to me about the few things that can't.

Back in the room

The way out of this isn't to burn it all down. No one can out-willpower a buffet built by 10 thousand engineers to keep us grabbing, and we shouldn't have to.

It isn't only me. Vinyl is outselling CDs again, and listening bars—rooms where a host plays records through good speakers and the only thing anyone does is sit and hear an album end-to-end—are opening in London and New York and Barcelona. People are paying for the one thing the content buffet made free and then made impossible: to be fully with a single thing. The fix they've rediscovered is the friction the buffet stripped away.

And the museum study already named the smaller, private version of it. The antidote was never about less music; it was the focused kind of attention that puts you all the way inside what you already have.

I recently changed one thing. This past Saturday, before I let myself hunt, I pulled up one of the forgotten strangers. It was an album I'd saved two years ago by an artist whose name meant little to me anymore. I put my phone face down and didn't save a single thing. I just listened, the whole way through.

Halfway in, a track did the thing, the chill down the spine, the exact feeling I've been chasing since I was 14. And there it was: I'd had it all along. I found that album once, saved it, and walked right past it on my way to find the feeling again.

I think many of us are living like that now, with most of what we love. We find it, save it, and walk right past it on the way to find it again. The weird mercy is how little it takes to stop. One thing, all the way through, before you reach for the next.

Watch the whole show before you queue up three more. Call the person on your mind, right now, before the next want takes over. The hunt is still the reward; the full listen is just the price of admission. And that small rule is the difference between collecting a life and living one.

So, yeah, I went right back to hunting. But I let that stranger keep playing.

item.title: Think You Don't Have a Type? Science Says You Probably Do
item.description:
Mating

Think You Don't Have a Type? Science Says You Probably Do

Research reveals surprising consistency in who we date and fall in love with.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows people’s exes and current partners often share similar personality traits.
  • A person's romantic partners tend to resemble each other physically more than random chance predicts.
  • People high in extraversion and openness to experience have less consistent "types" when it comes to dating.
Source: Photo by Giorgio Trovato on Unsplash

Think about your exes for a moment. Do they all seem completely different to you, or do you notice that they share certain traits?

The idea that people have a romantic "type" is deeply embedded in popular culture, but just how much commonality exists in the partners we select? In this post, we'll explore what the research says.

Do We Choose Partners With Similar Personalities?

In a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers at the University of Toronto analyzed data from a nine-year longitudinal study that involved a nationally representative sample of Germans. However, they only focused on the responses of 332 adults (159 men and 173 women) who had two different romantic partners to participate in this study at different points in time over that nine-year term.

Each individual—and each of their partners—were asked to complete the Big Five personality inventory, which assessed their standing on the traits of openness to experience, conscientiousness, agreeableness, extraversion, and neuroticism.

Researchers then looked to see whether the responses of people’s partners overlapped, and they did. In other words, people’s exes and current partners tended to have similar personality profiles.

It’s important to note that people’s own personality traits were also related to those of their partners. In other words, people tended to select partners who were similar to them. However, similarity between partners existed above and beyond similarity to the self. In other words, what we’re seeing here is indeed evidence that people are going for a certain “type,” as opposed to simply seeking out a like-minded partner.

That said, it’s worth mentioning that some personality traits were linked to having less consistency in one’s chosen partners. Specifically, those who were more extraverted (meaning they are outgoing and sociable) and those who were open to new experiences (meaning they like to try new and different things) didn’t seem to have as strong of a type. This makes sense because extraverts are likely to meet a wider range of people due to their outgoing nature, while those high in openness are just more willing to experiment and explore in general.

Do Our Romantic Partners Tend to Look Alike?

One limitation of the preceding research is that it only considered whether people tend to seek out a certain personality type. Do we tend to have a physical type as well?

A study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology considered the extent to which people’s previous partners “clustered” in terms of certain physical traits, such as attractiveness and masculinity. The results of this research revealed that people's past partners were more similar to one another in their physical traits than would be expected by chance.

article continues after advertisement

Together, these two sets of findings suggest that people tend to have both physical and personality types they tend to seek out in their romantic partners.

Implications

We need more research to know whether this tendency toward having a romantic type ultimately has positive or negative implications. On the one hand, knowing your type could help streamline the dating selection process, increasing the likelihood of pursuing relationships with the people who are most compatible with our preferences. But on the other hand, having a strong type could potentially narrow our dating pools in ways that don't serve us well. For example, we might end up overlooking partners who possess desirable qualities simply because they don't fit our typical mold. We need more research to better understand when having a type helps and when it holds us back.

That said, there are important implications of this line of work. One of the big ones is that our romantic choices may be more predictable than they appear at first glance. While we often think of attraction as spontaneous and unpredictable, the evidence suggests that we tend to gravitate to people with certain profiles.

This insight might prove useful in the world of online dating and matchmaking. Understanding the kinds of traits people have consistently been attracted to in the past (and the traits their previous partners have had in common) could potentially improve the quality of recommended matches. Whether that will ultimately lead to stronger relationships is an open question, but the existing evidence suggests that our dating pasts may contain important clues about our future romantic choices.

item.title: Change Your Life Story to Unroot Shame and Regret
item.description:
Self-Esteem

Change Your Life Story to Unroot Shame and Regret

Rewriting your life story can change it from critical to compassionate.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Childhood trauma often shapes a self-critical life story centered on shame and regret.
  • Kids blame themselves for neglect to protect attachment, fueling lifelong negative beliefs.
  • Examining key life events through journaling can uncover patterns in one's self-view.
Source: Etienne Girardet/Unsplash

Who do you think you are? When you look back at your life, what story do you tell about how you became the person you are today?

I’m guessing that, if you are like most of the people who have sat in my consulting room, this story is not a kind one. You may be laser-focused on everything that has been bad or wrong in your life, blaming yourself for every mistake, embarrassment, or crisis. You might describe yourself in horrible ways like "loser," "failure," or "pathetic." If so, I feel for you—this is no way to live.

But sadly, it’s incredibly common, especially if you experienced childhood trauma or neglect, and your needs were unmet on a regular basis. This would have had a profound effect on the way your developing mind made sense of the world. If you didn’t experience enough love, support, or safety, you may have explained that by thinking you were bad or wrong in some fundamental way. You might have felt flawed, unlikeable, or unlovable. You may have told a story in which you were always to blame, no matter what bad things happened to you. And as part of that story, you would have developed negative, self-critical beliefs about who you were.

Heartbreakingly, children tend to feel they are at fault for any negative experiences they have with their family. One of the most convincing theories for why kids make this choice is that they are protecting the attachment to their primary caregivers. Remember that these attachments are incredibly powerful for young children. We also know that the attachment system is linked to the amygdala, a part of the brain concerned with protecting us from life-threatening dangers. And this makes sense, because in the hunter-gatherer tribes from which we all evolved, if your parents didn’t attach to you as a baby, you wouldn’t last long.

Why abandonment is so terrifying

This is why your attachment system can fire up with what feels like life-or-death intensity—because for your ancestors, that was true. If you are a small child and, say, your mum is cold and disinterested, making you feel unimportant and unloved, it can be too threatening to think, "Maybe the problem is with her, because she’s so cold and unemotional. Maybe that’s why she can’t show her love to me." If that were true, you might feel alone and abandoned, left to fend for yourself in a scary world. So, it’s far safer for your little brain to think, "Maybe there’s something wrong with me; I’m too naughty, or not clever enough, or thin and pretty like my sister. Maybe if I can change, be better, smarter or skinnier, then she might love me."

Deeply sad, but true. And this is how these negative, self-lacerating stories begin to take shape in your mind. As a small child, you may not be conscious of these beliefs but instead just sense them as an inner knowing. And as an adult, you may have thought this way for so long that it feels true, deep in your gut.

article continues after advertisement

This post is all about the way this unhelpful story develops and, crucially, how you can begin telling a different story about your life. This new story is one in which, as I often explain to my clients: You are not a bad person; you’re a good person that bad things happened to. This shift is not easy, but it is possible. I profoundly believe that because I have helped so many people think differently about themselves, moving from a life filled with shame and regret to one that shines with self-compassion. That’s why I am confident you can do the same.

To change your life story, it's helpful to look at the current version—the one you have been telling yourself for decades. In this exercise, spend time journaling about the key events of your life. Imagine this is a movie and you’re the main character—what is the narrative arc? Starting with your earliest memories, or perhaps family stories about how you were as a child, ask yourself these questions, then write the answers in your journal. Remember there is no right or wrong way to do this, and be as honest as possible.

What is your life story?

Use the following questions to help with your exploration of the key events in your life:

  • What kind of baby do you think you were? When family members describe you, what do they say? That you were calm, happy, sweet, easy to care for—or that you cried a lot, didn’t sleep, were a "difficult" baby, or worse?
  • What were some of the key moments of your childhood? Are these happy memories, or unhappy ones? Think about foundational life events like your first day at school, birthdays, your first girlfriend/boyfriend, exam results and sporting events. Did they go well or badly? And if they went badly, how did your parents react? They may have criticized you or compared you unfavourably to your siblings or peers; if they did, do you now agree with them or think they were wrong?
  • Moving into adulthood, again focus on big life events—like going to university (if you went), getting married and having children (if you did), big losses in your life like bereavements or relationship breakups, periods of physical or mental ill-health, your job/career history, and key friendships. Do you beat yourself up about any of this, perhaps feeling regret, embarrassment or even shame?
  • Finally, what do you think you’re like? If you had to put this into a brief sentence, you might say: "I am ___." This might be kind/clever/funny/thoughtful or stupid/lazy/selfish/needy or some other negative description. There are no right or wrong answers; just be truthful. Your answer will reveal how you view yourself, and facing the reality of that is a key step on the road to healing and growth.
article continues after advertisement

This is an extract from my new book, Heal Your Trauma: How to Overcome a Painful Childhood to Become Happy and Whole Again.

item.title: Shame, Stigma, and the GLP-1 Treatment Journey
item.description:
Shame

Shame, Stigma, and the GLP-1 Treatment Journey

How stigma can subdue even the best weight loss treatments.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Shame and stigma are among the most powerful obstacles to a healthy weight loss journey.
  • Shame and stigma can be present before, during, and after weight loss in different ways.
  • GLP-1 medicines improve weight loss but introduce new sources of shame and stigma.

Marcus had practiced his answer before anyone asked the question. By the time a colleague stopped him in the hallway after a staff meeting, "Man, you look different. What are you doing?" he had a smooth response ready: cleaner eating, better sleep, less drinking. All of it true. Just incomplete.

"I told myself it was private, which it is," Marcus says now, several months into tirzepatide (a GLP-1 medicine). "But there's a difference between keeping something private and hiding something because you're ashamed of it."

Marcus is one of two composite patients, drawn from years of clinical work with people using GLP-1 medicines, whose stories anchor this piece on shame and stigma during GLP-1 treatment. The second is Diane, a cardiac nurse who has spent her career telling patients that obesity is biological, not a character flaw, and who is still working out how to extend that same belief to herself.

Two Forms of Stigma

Source: Thomas Rutledge / PowerPoint

Researchers distinguish between two forms of stigma.1 Enacted stigma arrives from outside: the raised eyebrow, the offhand comment, the relative who suggests you're taking the easy way out. Self-stigma is the critical inner voice that runs automatically even when no one else is around. Both forms are active throughout the GLP-1 journey. And they often show up more than once.

In clinical practice with GLP-1 medicines, four moments are influenced by stigma: (1) the decision to start treatment, (2) the social experience of using it, (3) the choice to continue long-term, and (least expected) (4) the moments when treatment is visibly succeeding.2 Marcus and Diane each lived through two of them.

1. The Gatekeeper: The Barrier to Starting

By the time Marcus seriously considered tirzepatide, he had already spent three months turning the decision over privately. He researched the way he approaches most things: mechanism first, evidence second. Intellectually, he was convinced.

What slowed him down was something he never mentioned to anyone, a moment catching his reflection in a mirrored gym wall during a student demonstration. The shame he felt from that brief moment paused him for months.

Like Marcus, most people arriving at a prescriber's office for a GLP-1 medicine are not encountering weight stigma for the first time. They are arriving with years of it already absorbed.3 The intake process itself, the weigh-in, the BMI conversation, can subtly reactivate that history before any prescription is written.

This pathway also runs in a direction patients rarely see: the clinician's side of the exam room. A provider's own unexamined assumptions about who will "comply," who has "really tried hard enough," or who "deserves" the medicine invisibly shape the conversation, whether or not they're spoken aloud.4

2. The Isolator: The Barrier to Social Support

Diane's version was hidden inside and lasted longer.

"I know better," she told her therapist early in treatment. "I literally teach this to my patients. I tell them it's biology, not willpower, and I mean every word of it. But when it's me, there's a voice that says I should have been able to do this on my own."

What makes this pathway distinct from the first is that the shame doesn't block the decision to start; it shapes what happens after. This is where stigma does some of its most consequential damage.2 Research on disclosure consistently finds that the extremes carry the most risk: (a) total concealment isolates a person from the social support that improves outcomes, while (b) indiscriminate openness exposes them to the full range of other people's unprocessed opinions. What tends to serve people best is something in between: deliberate, selective disclosure to a small number of people likely to respond with curiosity rather than judgment.

3. The Saboteur: The Barrier to Long-Term Commitment

Most people expect the "cheating" feeling to fade with time. For many, it does. Until it comes back.5

Eighteen months into treatment, Diane noticed her inner critic hadn't disappeared so much as hibernated. It resurfaced after an offhand comment from a relative she rarely sees: "Do you really need to take that forever?" Nothing about the question was hostile. It still hurt.

The useful response here is one Diane uses often: If a patient came to her with this exact biological picture, would she tell them they were taking the easy way out? Her answer is no, immediately, unequivocally. The gap between that answer and how she sometimes still talks to herself is not evidence she's failing at this. It's evidence that self-stigma doesn't resolve in one sitting. It must be responded to repeatedly and gradually replaced.

4. The Imposter: The Barrier to Internalizing Success

Return to the school hallway. Marcus had prepared for being asked about his weight loss. What he wasn't ready for was how the question itself would feel: genuinely admiring, yet somehow still loaded.

This is the pathway that surprises people most, because it inverts the expectation that stigma is something you escape by succeeding. "You look amazing; what are you doing?" for example, carries an implicit comment on how you looked before. Even warm, well-meant attention can feel like exposure when the change becomes visible faster than the person inside it has caught up.6

For Marcus, this was stigma showing up at the exact moment the treatment was demonstrably working, dressed as a compliment. Understanding this in advance doesn't make the moment painless. But it does change what the moment means: not evidence that something is wrong with how you're handling this, but a predictable feature of a culture still catching up to what successful treatment actually looks like from the inside.

A Reframe for a Rewarding GLP-1 Journey

Most people brace for shame and stigma the way they'd brace for a single difficult conversation: something to get through once before the "real" journey begins. The four pathways above suggest something less tidy yet more useful to know in advance. Stigma isn't a one-time visitor. It shows up at the start, during the middle, in the questions that resurface even years later, and sometimes precisely when things are outwardly going well. Each appearance can call for a different response, and expecting only one occurrence is part of why the second, third, or fourth can feel so disorienting when it arrives. The outcome is worth the work to get there.

item.title: Why Facts Rarely Change Political Polarization at Work
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Why Facts Rarely Change Political Polarization at Work

Bias and moral frameworks shape how we view coworkers with different beliefs.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Outgroup homogeneity bias makes people assume opposing political groups are more uniform than they are.
  • Morality-as-cooperation theory explains how shared social instincts lead to different political values.
  • Facts and logic rarely change minds; genuine curiosity and empathy are more effective.

It’s no secret that we live in a world where people are frequently polarized in their political views. In the United States, Republicans and Democrats are frequently seen as opposites with virtually no overlapping values. Indeed, it has devolved into members of each political party calling members of the other immoral or evil, and “conservative” and “liberal” have become derogatory labels. This extreme perspective can leave coworkers feeling alienated from those who do not share their political affiliation or general set of values.

Let’s turn to psychology to help understand what is going on. First, consider the outgroup homogeneity bias. This refers to the universal, and apparently innate, tendency for people to view members of groups to which they themselves do not belong (outgroups) as more similar to each other compared to how they view members of their own groups (ingroups). In other words, we more easily recognize the diversity across those who comprise our ingroups than we do our outgroups. This makes it easy to describe everyone in the “other” group in concise ways that do not reflect reality.

Applying this phenomenon to politics, Republicans view Democrats as all sharing a particular set of beliefs and values, but recognize that among Republicans there is a good deal of variation. Of course, the same tendency applies to Democrats when they think and talk about Republicans. The outgroup homogeneity bias helps ensure continued polarization, as we fail to recognize that not all Republicans and not all Democrats think alike. So, we likely are closer in opinions and values to at least some members of the other party than we assume we are.

How Morality-as-Cooperation Theory Explains Political Values

Next, let’s examine the foundation for liberal versus conservative values. Morality-as-cooperation (MAC) theory describes that humans, through the long process of evolution, became equipped with inherent approaches to how to relate and cooperate with each other. These approaches include preferring to allocate resources to kin, working together for a shared cause, coordinating social exchange for fairness, recognition of prior possession, and avoiding and resolving conflict through displays of bravery, dominance, or submission. These approaches are universal, but each individual prioritizes and applies them differently, which helps explain differences in political values.

Typically (but not always) conservatives most value family, patriotism, the military and law enforcement agencies, a strong border, and lower taxes. Viewed through the lens of MAC theory, such individuals prioritize allocating resources to kin (support for family), avoiding and resolving conflict through displays of bravery or dominance (patriotism and military) or submission (deference to authority and hierarchy), and recognition of prior possession (resistance to taxation).

Typically (but not always) liberals most value care for others (including non-kin and the environment that is left to future generations), egalitarianism, and equity in distribution of resources. Viewed through the lens of MAC theory, such individuals prioritize coordinating social exchange for fairness (a strong social safety net through taxing wealth, respecting individual rights across diversity), and recognition of prior possession (support for the rights of indigenous peoples and those whose history was slavery).

Notice that liberals and conservatives share emphasis on some of the same values, but those values are applied or expressed differently. For example, recognition of prior possession can be applied to one’s own possessions (strong property rights) or the original possessors of some resource (indigenous peoples’ claims to land, or slaves’ claims to the output of their labor). Expression of the approach to ensuring fairness may take the form of being concerned over whether some people are receiving government benefits who do not deserve them or take the form of believing that it is unfair that some people have so much while others suffer without enough. And, both conservatives and liberals believe in working together for a shared cause, yet those causes sometimes differ, and so different groups form to promote those causes (e.g., family values, reproductive freedom, gun rights, environmental protection).

Frequently, liberals and conservatives label members of the other group as immoral. Instead, it appears that each group has a different definition of morality. I personally believe that virtually every American sees themselves as moral and wants what’s best for the country. The disconnect comes from the details behind those general convictions (what is moral, and what is best for our country). Then the differences are highlighted and incorporated into the social identities of those who take on a social label, with mass media eager to reinforce the idea that membership in one camp means being embattled in an existential struggle with fellow Americans wearing the other label (see this explanation).

How to Relate to Coworkers With Different Political Views

So, with regard to coworkers with different political views, what can you do?

  1. Recognize that everyone is the hero in their own story. It’s easy to feel self-righteous and villainize another person. The challenge is in recognizing their shared humanity; everyone wants to be happy and wants to have a country of which they can be proud. We all share the same underlying set of approaches for interacting as members of a society (the MAC theory), but we differ in how we prioritize those approaches and how each is expressed.
  2. Recognize the reality of the outgroup homogeneity bias. I imagine that as you read my general description of “typical” liberals and conservatives, you bristled at my characterization of whichever group with which you identify. Why? Because you recognize how crude my description was in light of the individual variation that actually exists. Look for that diversity among the coworkers who do not share your political views. It’s natural to focus on their differences from you. The challenge is to intentionally look for similarities, which likely exist in abundance beyond the domains of “liberal” vs. “conservative” or Republican vs. Democrat.
  3. Consider the results of research on influencing another person’s opinions. Using facts, logic, and argument does not work. Why? Our self-identity is tied to our beliefs, and when they are challenged, we double down. Instead, try genuine interest in understanding the other person’s perspective; exactly what it is, where it came from, and why it’s important to them. Research indicates that genuine curiosity results in the other person lowering their defenses and, ultimately, being more open to considering differing views.

In the end, you and your coworkers will never see eye to eye, but hopefully it helps to realize that we share a mental framework that has allowed humans to live in groups for a very long time. Where the differences lie is in relative priority and how we apply or express those underlying approaches to morality.

item.title: AI and Your Cognitive Fingerprint
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI and Your Cognitive Fingerprint

It's time to ask where your thinking is actually coming from.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • AI can generate excellent answers, making it harder to know whether genuine thinking occurred.
  • The most important ideas often emerge through questioning, uncertainty, and cognitive friction.
  • Our cognitive fingerprint may reveal the human thinking behind the response.
Source: Kris / Pixabay

I do a lot of thinking about thinking. So when artificial intelligence (AI) started producing answers that were genuinely good, I wasn't too worried about the answers themselves. I was worried about our ability to think.

This concern has escalated. AI gets it done, from an email to a clinical diagnosis to business strategy. And the output can often be excellent. But that's precisely the problem, because the artifact no longer tells you much about the person presenting it. Does today's AI output tell about the user or obscure that person behind a digital facade?

Questions and Answers

Voltaire said that we shouldn't judge people by their answers but by their questions. The attribution is uncertain, but the insight is spot on. But here's something almost counterintuitive about it, as we've always rewarded answers. School, work, and thought-leadership are largely organized around the production of correct responses. Questions were the stepping stone and answers the destination. But that hierarchy had a built-in assumption: Answers were hard to come by. They no longer are. Which means the question may become the more revealing signal.

The Value of Friction

The Greeks understood something about this. Socrates wasn't trying to get to the right answer in the most efficient way. He was trying to expose the struggle and push people to new perspectives. The friction in those dialogues wasn't incidental; it was the point.

Modern culture has developed a fairly aggressive relationship with that kind of friction. We've built systems, habits, and now technologies oriented around its elimination. And all of this is done in the name of improvement and advancement. Some evidence suggests that the gains in speed may be coming with cognitive costs.

I think that something else has happened alongside that. As we embrace the artifact of the output, questioning itself has been repositioned. Push back on an idea, and you're not engaging but attacking. Ask for evidence, and you're being hostile. We've arrived at a strange moment where the very act of inquiry carries social risk. A point where "your truth" has become a kind of armor against scrutiny. Instant gratification didn't just shorten our attention spans; it made depth feel like something of an imposition.

AI arrives into a world already primed to receive answers without friction, and where people are increasingly suspicious of anyone who asks why.

AI and Ownership

But AI did something else. It exposed a confusion that was already underway. For years, we've been moving toward a world where producing something and understanding it are treated as the same thing. Let's be clear: They're not.

article continues after advertisement

And the examples abound. A student generates an essay that perfectly aligns with the academic rubric. A consultant hands over a smart and polished deck. A manager presents a strategy complete with a tactical roll-out. In each case, the output may be impressive. The critical question that's harder to answer is whether the person behind it did anything more than receive it.

The Cognitive Fingerprint

We've seen the use of the watermark to validate the provenance of an image. In this context, I've started thinking about this as the cognitive fingerprint.

It's not a stamp of ownership, but something more specific. It's the trace left behind when an idea has actually passed through a mind. It appears when someone can explain their perspective. And in that context, it's that "dialogue" that articulates the cognitive path that resulted in the conclusion.

The cognitive fingerprint validates not the work, but the thinker.

The Wrong Question

Whether someone used AI is the wrong question. The right question is whether the person has developed any real ownership of the ideas they're presenting—those are different things. You can possess a conclusion without understanding it, and you can repeat an argument without making it yours.

The stakes are real across every domain I can think of. A physician who retrieves information faster than anyone in the room may be the least valuable person in a diagnostic conversation. A scientist who answers quickly may be asking the wrong question entirely. A business analyst who produces the most thorough report may have buried the one assumption that invalidates it. Standing under the bright light of an answer requires more than possession; it requires ownership.

What's Scarce Now

Maybe the cognitive fingerprint is less a mark than a trace.

Because today, answers have become abundant. They're cheap, fast, and often very good. What's becoming scarce is the person who shows you, in how they negotiate an idea, that it actually traversed a mind that gave it meaning.

item.title: The Real Reason Behind Kids' Attention-Seeking Behavior
item.description:
Parenting

The Real Reason Behind Kids' Attention-Seeking Behavior

The need for daily one-on-one time can lead kids to act out.

Posted June 23, 2026

Key points
  • Attention-seeking behavior in kids often signals a need for connection with their parent.
  • Children prefer a parent's playful attention, but they'll settle for frustrated attention.
  • Ten minutes of daily one-on-one time addresses the root of many attention-seeking behaviors in kids.

This post is part 1 of a series.

Your child has been following you around all morning. You've heard, "Play with meeee" for what seems like the hundredth time. You're exhausted before the day has even started.

It's easy to look at that and think: I need to set a better boundary. But you've already set it, and they're not stopping. So what's actually going on?

Attention-Seeking Behavior Is a Signal

When children show attention-seeking behavior—melting down, refusing to cooperate, climbing all over you while you're trying to drink your coffee—they're usually signaling a need for connection with you. This is especially common with attention-seeking behavior in preschoolers, whose ability to just say, "I miss you, I need more of you," is still developing. When that need isn't being met consistently, children find ways to meet it—and it often involves doing things you don't like.

But children don't always seek connection in ways that look like connection. In her book, Hold Me Tight, Sue Johnson describes a wife who would deliberately pick fights with her husband. She explains: When he was disengaged, she didn't know if he cared. When he fought back, she knew he did. Children operate the same way. They'd prefer the fun, playful version of your attention. But they'll take the frustrated "please stop doing that" over nothing at all.

When you see it that way, the behavior looks different. You understand that it’s a bid for connection, expressed in the only language available to them right now.

How Do I Emotionally Connect With My Child?

One of the most effective tools for building connection is also one of the simplest: dedicated one-on-one time. This is called "Special Time"—a short, predictable block of time, ideally daily, where you give your child your complete, undivided attention. No phone. No half-listening while you unload the dishwasher. During this time, your child leads and you follow.

You might already be spending a lot of time with your child—feeding them, driving them, reading to them at night. But none of that counts as Special Time, because during all of it, you're still the one in charge. Special Time is different because your child is in charge.

Is One-on-One Time Good for Kids?

Children have a deep need for connection with their parents. When your child gets your full, undivided attention regularly, it addresses the root of a lot of difficult behavior at home because the need driving that behavior is already being met.

Family quality time—shared meals, outings, game nights—has real value, too. But it doesn't replace one-on-one time, because during group time, your child is still sharing you. Special Time is theirs alone.

How Much One-on-One Time Does a Child Need?

Ten minutes per child per day is a realistic starting point for most families. That might sound like either too little or too much depending on where you are right now. But consistency is what makes this work. A predictable 10 minutes every day will do more for your parenting relationship than an occasional long stretch that only happens when you can get to it.

Your child will protest at the end of their first Special Time. They might even have a meltdown. They will really love Special Time, and they won’t want it to end.

Why would I recommend a practice that generates meltdowns? Because when you make Special Time consistent, the meltdowns stop. At the end of the 10 minutes, you’ll say: “Special Time is over for today. We’ll have it again tomorrow.” When it happens again tomorrow, and the next day, your child will trust that it will come again tomorrow, and the protests will stop.

Two Ways to Make It Predictable

  1. Anchor it to a fixed point in the day. Right after the baby goes down for a nap. After dinner is on the stove. It doesn't have to be the same time every single day—a weekday plan and a weekend plan both work, as long as you and your child both know what to expect.

  2. Say yes when they ask. If you're not on a call and there's no urgent reason to say no, saying yes in that moment builds trust fast. We're trained to work first and play later. But that sends a message to children: Work is always more important than you. Flipping that sends a different message entirely, and it builds your parenting relationship in ways that pay off all day long.

Final Thoughts

Attention-seeking behavior is exhausting, precisely because it doesn't stop until the need driving it gets met. Special Time works because it gets ahead of that. Ten consistent minutes of one-on-one time, every day, signals to your child: You don't have to work so hard to get my attention. It's already yours.

In Part 2, we'll get into the five specific practices that make Special Time actually work—and what to do if you're a parent who struggles to be present, even when you're trying.
